questions.stem: Which sequence correctly represents the evolution of Wi-Fi security and its encryption?
questions.explanation: The progression is WEP (obsolete) to WPA with TKIP, then WPA2 and WPA3 which both use the strong AES cipher.
questions.trap: TKIP belongs to the early WPA stopgap, not to WEP or WPA3. WPA2/WPA3 use AES.

questions.stem: Which encryption cipher do BOTH WPA2 and WPA3 rely on?
questions.explanation: WPA2 and WPA3 both use AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), the strong modern cipher.
questions.trap: TKIP was the legacy WPA1 stopgap cipher for older hardware; it is not what WPA2/WPA3 use.

questions.stem: Which is a security advantage of WPA3 over WPA2 highlighted in the review?

choices.text: It downgrades encryption to TKIP for compatibility
It removes the need for any password ever
It only works on wired connections
It strengthens the initial key exchange and can encrypt even open public networks

questions.explanation: WPA3 still uses AES but strengthens the initial key exchange and can provide encryption even on open public networks.
questions.trap: WPA3 does not fall back to TKIP; downgrading to TKIP would weaken, not strengthen, security.

questions.stem: A company wants each Wi-Fi user to authenticate with a unique username and password checked against a central server. Which mode should they deploy?

choices.text: Enterprise mode (802.1X) with a RADIUS server

questions.explanation: Enterprise mode (802.1X) requires a unique username/password per user, validated against a central authentication server, usually RADIUS.
questions.trap: Personal/PSK mode shares one password among everyone - the opposite of per-user credentials.

questions.stem: A home user sets one Wi-Fi password that everyone in the house shares. What is this authentication method called?
questions.explanation: A pre-shared key (Personal mode) is the single shared password model - like one key to the front door that everyone uses.
questions.trap: Enterprise mode/802.1X requires unique per-user credentials, not a single shared key.

questions.stem: Which protocol is the most common centralized AAA server, called on by Wi-Fi, VPN, and switches to verify credentials?
questions.explanation: RADIUS is the common AAA protocol that Wi-Fi, VPN, and switches call to centrally verify credentials.
questions.trap: Kerberos provides SSO inside a Windows domain; it is not the device-facing AAA server in this scenario.

questions.stem: Which authentication protocol provides single sign-on in a Windows domain using a ticket-granting system and mutual authentication?
questions.explanation: Kerberos enables SSO in a Windows domain: you log in once, receive a ticket, and present it to other resources. It provides mutual authentication.
questions.trap: TACACS+ is an AAA protocol associated with Cisco hardware; it is not the Windows-domain SSO ticket system.

questions.stem: Which AAA protocol is described as similar to RADIUS but heavily associated with Cisco hardware?
questions.explanation: TACACS+ is a similar but less common AAA protocol, heavily associated with Cisco hardware.
questions.trap: RADIUS is the more common AAA option; the Cisco-associated one is TACACS+.

questions.stem: In the AAA framework, what does the second 'A' (Authorization) define?

choices.text: Proving you are who you say you are
What resources you are allowed to access

questions.explanation: Authorization defines what you can access. Authentication proves identity, and Accounting tracks activity.
questions.trap: Proving identity is Authentication (the first A); tracking activity is Accounting (the third A).

questions.stem: Why was TKIP introduced as part of the original WPA?

choices.text: It was the strongest cipher ever created
It was designed only for WPA3 open networks
It was a stopgap that could run on older hardware unable to handle stronger encryption
It was required for wired Ethernet

questions.explanation: TKIP was a crucial stopgap because it could run on older hardware that could not handle stronger encryption like AES.
questions.trap: TKIP is not the strongest cipher - AES replaced it precisely because TKIP was a temporary measure.
